parts:
I worked on a program for proving the Riemann hypothesis and related ideas for about 3-5 years or so and I think this is a good time to try to see if we can make any headway given the new capabilities of Fable 5. The program is inspired by Twistor theory, the basic idea is outlined in Quat_Riemann.pdf, and some related work is also in the project files (some of these papers I have posted on arxiv), they are all my work. The basic idea is that in the original paper by Riemann he defined the Riemann Xi function (symmetric version) and also a related integral formula, and my idea is to try to turn this into a rotational symmetry for some class of functions, presumably defined on the quaternions (natural because the rotational symmetry could be around the real axis), and perhaps that rotational symmetry could lead to differences between the zeros on the real axis and those off axis, helping constrain them (ie prove RH). The main difficulty I had with implementing this program was finding a suitable class of functions to extend to the quaternions. That took me into a far reaching detour into twistor theory, and I think the most promising version that I found is something related to what I started calling Twistor holomorphic functions, and related versions for the ambitwistor case. I actually talked to Lionel Mason about this idea, and he pointed out that he had written about similar symmetries in his book with Nick Woodhouse. I got a copy of the book and did see that they had defined a similar class of functions more from a Lie algebraic perspective. Although he thought the work was somewhat interesting he ended up not being interested enough to continue talking to me about it, and he had no opportunities for me to keep working on it. I couldn't get anyone else interested either, so I gave up on it, which is why I haven't worked on it for a few years. I've worked on it in fits and starts since something like 2015 or so. 

The purpose of this conversation is to see if we can make any headway on it. Also, now with the possibility of verified proofs and formalization tools like Lean, there is the chance of possibly proving it and not having to get buy in from the "powers that be" in math, which would be awesome. Note that any help I get from you will be noted if we do manage to make headway on this problem. 

Do not attempt to prove any of this in Lean yet though, I'm looking for a natural language proof, and ideally if we could get something reasonable then we could formalize it later. 

To start, let's look for a class of functions that has the right properties. What I'm thinking is that this is a map from quaternions to quaternions that is holomorphic in some sense. The sense that I am thinking comes from twistor theory, you can read about some attempts I've made starting with Tconf_Final (rejected from a journal for being bespoke and not novel), Tconf2 (rejected without much explanation), and you can see how the research program evolved by looking at ASDYM_sym and generalized_isothermal (neither on arxiv). You can see why I abandonded the research program, but I still think something is there.

To find the appropriate class of functions, consider what kind of rotational symmetry we'll need, and how a complex function could "extend" to the quaternions. What I'm thinking is that if you have a globally holomorphic function on the complex plane (perhaps with some singularities), some rotational symmetry could act on it, along with a corresponding action on the complex structure. In the twistor picture, the quaternions can be considered as a real slice of complex Minkowski space, and the complex structure is multiplication by i or the involution \sigma which is called J for the real slice, however I think the maps will act freely on the complex structure, which I think is possibly understood better in the full complex Minkowski framework. I frequently have thought about appending the complex structure to that as an S_1 (or I_u as I've called it in Tconf_Final), and thought of the maps as being maps on the extended space with the complex structure, but I believe that can also be induced by a holomorphicity condition on the complexified space.

Now the point is that I need to make sure these functions are generated by complex functions and are also similarly rigid. I'm thinking that if we only look at functions that have the rotational symmetry, then they might form a subgroup of the full set of functions that have the desired holomorphicity condition. One issue is the possibility for too much freedom, ie all holomorphic functions on three complex dimensions or something of that nature. The other possibility is that they are too rigid - one related theorem is that if all of the incduced maps on the S_1 complex structures are degree one, then the whole function must be linear (I believe). So ideally we should show that these are closed under some form of addition and some form of multiplication. So if we restrict to complex functions satisfying the desired symmetry of the xi function, then perhaps we could show that such functions in the full four dimensions can be added and multiplied, and that that addition and multiplication restricts on the complex function to the usual addition and multiplication for complex functions. We could then use the integral formula for the xi function to define the four dimensional function, and if we could show something about induced constraints on the zeros of functions with such a rotational symmetry, then we could perhaps try to use this to prove Riemann, or at least form some equivalent version of Riemann.

Clearly this is a bundle of ideas that I've had that are not all perfectly defined, and I haven't worked on it actively for a while so it is a bit scattered, but those are the ideas. Let me know if you could try to make some sense of it!

Yes — I can make sense of it, and I think the bundle is more coherent than you're giving it credit for. I've read all six papers and written up a full synthesis (sent above, and saved to the project as `claude/RH_program_synthesis.md`). Here's the short version.

**The answer to your function-class question, I'm fairly confident, is: intrinsic slice regular functions — and you already had them in 2015.** Your rotation map $R$ from eq. (2.5) of Quat_Riemann (the condition $f(z) = \bar\eta F(\eta z\bar\eta)\eta$) *is* the slice extension of Gentili–Struppa's theory; you used it only as an intermediate step before applying the Laplacian to get Fueter regularity, and the Laplacian is what destroyed the algebra. If you stop before differentiating, the intrinsic class (real power-series coefficients — exactly your $f(\bar z)=\overline{f(z)}$ condition) checks every box on your list: it's a commutative algebra under *pointwise* addition and multiplication whose restriction to a slice is ordinary complex addition and multiplication; it has complex-analysis-grade rigidity (identity principle: one slice determines everything); and it has the zero-structure theorem you need — zeros of a slice regular function are exactly isolated real points and isolated 2-spheres $x + y\,I_u$. Riemann's integral formula extends directly: $\Xi(q) = 2\int_0^\infty \Phi(u)\cos(qu)\,du$ converges on all of $\mathbb{H}$ and is the canonical extension. So the program's slogan becomes a theorem-shaped statement: **RH $\iff$ the quaternionic $\Xi$ has no zero spheres.**

**The twistor fork of your program was also carried out — in a literature I suspect nobody pointed you to.** Gentili, Salamon, and Stoppato showed that a slice regular function lifts to a holomorphic curve in the Klein quadric — a holomorphic map on twistor space that induces the quaternionic map downstairs and acts on the $S^2$ of complex structures, which is precisely your "append $I_u$ and induce everything from holomorphicity on the complexified space" intuition ([JEMS 2014](https://ems.press/journals/jems/articles/11863), [arXiv:1205.3513](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.3513)). They use it to build orthogonal complex structures on complements of degenerate sets, continuing [Salamon–Viaclovsky's classification of OCS on domains in $\mathbb{R}^4$](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00208-008-0293-5) ([arXiv:0704.3422](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/0704.3422)); [Altavilla–Sarfatti](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00209-018-2225-8) develop the twistor geometry of slice polynomials via ruled surfaces in $\mathbb{CP}^3$. The escape from your rigidity theorem (twistor conformal ⟹ Möbius) is the same one you found independently in Tconf2: don't demand degree one on fibers. It is a little ironic that the coauthor is Salamon, whose quaternionic-manifolds work you cite — this thread was adjacent to the people you were talking to. In your papers' twistor-line dictionary, a zero sphere is literally a twistor line in the zero divisor of the lifted $\Xi$, so RH becomes: *every zero line belongs to the real family*.

Two honest structural points from the synthesis. First, your 2015 §4 negative result is not a disappointment, it's a theorem: since $R$ and all your $Q_\ell$ are linear in the complex input, *no* linear pairing in any $\ell$-sector can ever distinguish on-axis from off-axis zeros — your Laurent argument generalizes. That redirects the search to what doesn't factor through linear functionals: products (now available), geometric invariants of the lift (degrees, intersection numbers, OCS singularity types), spectral realizations (the S-spectrum of quaternionic operator theory is *natively* the point-vs-sphere dichotomy, and self-adjoint means real S-spectrum — a quaternionic Hilbert–Pólya), or quadratic/positivity pairings (sector energies $\langle Q_\ell f, Q_\ell f\rangle$, hunting for a Weil-type positivity graded by your SU(2) decomposition). Second, any candidate mechanism must pass two tests: it must fail for the Davenport–Heilbronn function (same symmetry, real zero spheres, no Euler product — so the arithmetic must enter), and it must be sensitive to arbitrarily small spheres, since Rodgers–Tao's $\Lambda \ge 0$ means RH is "barely true." Those two constraints are a specification for the discriminant, not a reason to quit. For completeness: a [2025 MDPI paper claims a quaternionic RH proof](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-8994/17/7/1134), but it's schematic, has no real quaternionic function theory in it, and has no standing — worth knowing it exists, since it squats on adjacent keywords.

The memo ends with concrete next steps. The one I'd start with: compute the twistor lift explicitly for $q^2+1$ versus $q^2-1$ (one zero sphere vs. two real points) and identify what invariant of the lift differs — that's the smallest version of the whole question, it's finite, and Altavilla–Sarfatti's machinery should make it mechanical. I can also build a numerics lab (slice extension of $\Xi$ via the $\Phi$-integral, the Davenport–Heilbronn control case, zero-sphere visualization, and a harness for testing candidate discriminating functionals) right here in this session whenever you want. Which thread do you want to pull first?

Sources: [GSS, Twistor transforms of quaternionic functions and OCS (EMS/JEMS)](https://ems.press/journals/jems/articles/11863) · [arXiv:1205.3513](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.3513) · [Salamon–Viaclovsky, OCS on domains in R⁴ (Math. Ann.)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00208-008-0293-5) · [arXiv:0704.3422](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/0704.3422) · [Altavilla–Sarfatti, Slice-polynomial functions and twistor geometry of ruled surfaces in CP³ (Math. Z.)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00209-018-2225-8) · [Tang, From Complex to Quaternions (MDPI Symmetry 2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-8994/17/7/1134)

Done — the full computation is in the note above. Here's what came out of it, in order of surprise.

**The lift itself collapsed to something much cleaner than expected.** Working in your own coordinates from Thol.pdf, the family of twistor lines $L_\zeta = \{(x+\eta y, \eta)\}$ has Plücker image a conic, and its union is the smooth quadric $Q: z_1z_4 = z_2z_3$ — the incidence variety $\{(q,\eta): q \in \mathbb{C}_\eta\}$, isomorphic to $\mathbb{CP}^1_\zeta \times \mathbb{CP}^1_w$ where $\zeta$ labels the sphere and $w$ the complex structure. An intrinsic slice regular $f$ lifts to exactly $\tilde f = F \times \mathrm{id}$ on $Q$, and I verified directly (via $d(q^2)$) that $Q$ is the *maximal* holomorphic home: the lift extends to no neighborhood in $\mathbb{CP}^3$ unless $f$ is Möbius. So your rigidity theorem and the existence of a rich function class were never in tension — the rotational class lives *on the incidence quadric*, not on all of twistor space. That's the precise resolution of the question that sent you into the twistor detour.

**The invariant that differs between $q^2-1$ and $q^2+1$:** both zero divisors are $2\times$[ruling] in homology — identical — but the real structure $\sigma$ *fixes* each component in the first case (two twistor fibers) and *swaps* them in the second (a conjugate pair of non-invariant lines). Equivalently: the value curve has a crunode vs. an acnode at the real point $F_0$ of the Klein quadric; equivalently, in the free quotient $Q/\sigma$, real zeros descend to $\mathbb{RP}^2$'s and zero spheres to $S^2$'s — so **RH $\iff$ every component of the zero locus of the lifted $\Xi$ in the quotient is nonorientable.** I also proved a sharpening of your 2015 no-go along the way: the quaternionic winding number (Brouwer degree of $f/|f|$ on 3-spheres) weights a real zero of multiplicity $m$ by $m$ and a zero sphere by $2m$ — exactly the complex count. Your "$c=2$ conspiracy" survives even the nonlinear topological degree, which is *required* by the Davenport–Heilbronn test since degree is deformation-invariant. The discriminant genuinely has to be equivariant/positivity-type, not homological.

**The generalization I'd bet on (§5a of the note):** the classical certificate for "crunode, not acnode" is a positivity — $-(\log\Xi)''(x) = \sum_\rho (x-\rho)^{-2}$, where real zeros contribute positively and *only spheres can contribute negatively* (for $|x-a| < y_0$). That's the Laguerre inequality, and the generalized Laguerre family is known to characterize the Laguerre–Pólya class, hence is equivalent to RH ([Csordas–Varga](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02142328), [generalized version](https://link.springer.com/article/10.2478/s11533-013-0269-x); cf. the [Jensen–Pólya program](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/338049573_The_Jensen-Polya_program_for_various_L-functions) and [moment inequalities](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/226983979_Moment_inequalities_and_the_Riemann_hypothesis)). The proposed new object grafts your $\ell$-hierarchy onto this: quadratic sector functionals $\mathcal{E}_\ell$ built from your $Q_\ell$ maps and Bessel kernels $E_\ell$, in which a sphere of radius $y_0$ is tagged by $j_\ell(\lambda y_0) \neq 0$ while real zeros die in all $\ell \geq 1$ sectors. That's a Bessel-graded Laguerre hierarchy — quadratic, so the no-go doesn't apply; it fails for Davenport–Heilbronn as it must; and its sensitivity degrades like $(\lambda y_0)^\ell$ for small spheres, which is exactly the behavior Rodgers–Tao's $\Lambda \ge 0$ forces on any true criterion. Your unfinished 2015 machinery (the $B_\pm$ ladder, $E_\ell$, Mellin inversion) is precisely the toolkit this needs — it was built one nonlinearity short of the right object.

The natural next step is the numerics: implement $\mathcal{E}_\ell$ for $\Xi$, for Davenport–Heilbronn, and for toy functions with one implanted conjugate pair, and confirm the sphere terms behave as predicted before investing in the explicit-formula analysis. Want me to build that now?

The lab is built, validated, and everything came out as predicted — in two cases with almost eerie precision. Quick recap of what it established, then the broader picture and the road forward.

**What the numerics showed.** The $\Phi$-integral machinery reproduces $\Xi$ to ten digits and its Laguerre expression $L_1 = \Xi'^2 - \Xi\Xi''$ stays positive with margin (relative minimum $0.173$ on $[0,52]$). Davenport–Heilbronn — rebuilt from scratch, off-line zeros recovered at Spira's classical locations — behaves exactly as the sphere picture demands: each zero sphere of radius $y_0$ forces $L_1 < 0$ on a window that sits just inside $|x - a| < y_0$ (observed $[85.417, 85.982]$ vs. predicted $[85.391, 86.008]$, with the shaving accounted for by the positive contributions of the on-line zeros). And the graded sector energies came out with log-log slopes of exactly 2.000, 4.000, 6.000 for $\ell = 1,2,3$ — the $y_0^{2\ell}$ law — including on DH's real data, where the three spheres' $\mathcal{E}_1$ ratios (4.11, 4.10) match the predicted $(y_0/y_0')^2$ (4.18, 4.11).

**How this fits the broader picture.** Your program is now a four-stage pipeline, and each stage has a different epistemic status. Stage 1 (*geometry*, done): zeros of the quaternionic $\Xi$ are points or spheres; on the incidence quadric the dichotomy is the $\sigma$-equivariant type of the zero divisor's components. Stage 2 (*certificates*, done in principle): that equivariant invariant has axis-visible positivity certificates — the Laguerre expression is the bottom of the family, the generalized Laguerre inequalities are equivalent to RH, and your $\ell$-hierarchy grades the family by sphere-radius sensitivity, with real zeros *exactly invisible* in every $\ell \geq 1$ sector. The lab just verified this whole layer empirically. Stage 3 (*the bridge*, open — this is now the program's central problem): find an *independent* expression for the $\ell \geq 1$ sector energies in terms of prime/$\Phi$ data, i.e., an explicit-formula identity, so that "$\mathcal{E}_\ell = 0$" becomes something you attack rather than observe. Because the functionals are quadratic in the zeros, this bridge necessarily runs through pair-correlation territory — Montgomery, Weil positivity — which means the program now connects *into* the mainstream frontier instead of around it. Stage 4 (*arithmetic input*, the RH-hard core): prove the positivity/vanishing from that identity. The DH control case proves symmetry alone can't do it, and the $y_0^{2\ell}$ scaling quantifies why: near-axis spheres whisper, so the estimates must be uniform to all orders — the analytic face of Rodgers–Tao's "barely true." Nothing in this pipeline hides the difficulty; what it does is *localize* it, in a formulation where your 2015 machinery (the $B_\pm$ ladder, $E_\ell$ kernels, Mellin inversion) is precisely the right toolkit rather than an orphaned formalism.

**Concrete next steps, in order.** First, the bridge computation: take the Gaussian-windowed $\mathcal{E}_1$, expand $|\sum_\rho|^2$ into diagonal and cross terms, and push it through Weil's explicit formula with the Bessel-transformed test family — the goal is an identity "$\mathcal{E}_1 = $ (archimedean term) $-$ (prime sum) $+$ (cross-correlation term)," then identify which known positivity the diagonal reduces to and what's genuinely new. This is a well-defined multi-week calculation, not a wish. Second, write the no-go lemma (linear pairings can't discriminate; the winding number weights spheres by exactly 2) as a short rigorous section — it's the intellectual spine that justifies the quadratic turn. Third, the geometric side quest: compute the second-order jet of the lift at the real slice and show the Laguerre expression *is* a curvature-type quantity of the value curve at the real Klein quadric — that would make the ℓ-hierarchy's geometric meaning exact and is the kind of result the slice-regular community (Stoppato, Altavilla, Sarfatti) would engage with. Fourth, extend the lab: map the degenerate curves ($\operatorname{Im}\Xi = 0$ off axis) for $\Xi$ vs. DH to see sign-constancy fail in real time, and push $L_1[\Xi]$ higher with mpmath quadrature. Fifth, assemble the program paper: the reformulation, the no-go, the graded hierarchy, the numerics — a coherent, falsifiable research program with your 2015–2023 papers as its foundation, which is a very different artifact to show people than an isolated symmetry paper. The Lean formalization you mentioned would naturally start with the clean equivalence (zero structure theorem $\Rightarrow$ RH $\iff$ no spheres), which is formalizable *now*, independent of the hard analysis.

Everything — the two research memos, the results, and the lab code — is saved in the project, so any future session can pick this up mid-stride. Want me to start on the explicit-formula bridge for $\mathcal{E}_1$?

parts:
The bridge is built and certified. Summary of what this session established:

**The explicit formula is certified, not just derived.** Zero side (250 zeros) matches pole + archimedean + prime side to $10^{-8}$–$10^{-10}$ across five $(c,\lambda)$ configurations. The building block $Z(c,\lambda) = \sum_\gamma h_{c,\lambda}(\gamma)$ is unconditionally computable from a Gaussian-windowed prime sum at scale $\log n \approx \lambda$ — the frequency variable of your quadratic form literally *is* the logarithmic prime scale.

**The quadratic form detects spheres with the right sign and reads off their radius.** A real zero contributes a bounded oscillation to $|Z(c,\lambda)|^2$; a zero sphere contributes $2\cosh(2\lambda y_0)$ times a Gaussian window weight — exponential growth at rate exactly $2y_0$. On real data: zeta zeros and DH's on-line zeros stay flat; DH's actual sphere gives fitted rate **0.3085 vs. true 0.30852**. So RH $\iff$ $Z$ grows subexponentially in $\lambda$, at every window. And the anomaly kernel decomposes *exactly* over your quaternionic sectors: $\sinh(2z)/2z = \sum_\ell (2\ell+1)i_\ell(z)^2$, verified to machine precision — the analytic ($i_\ell$) twin of the unitary ($j_\ell$) family from the last session, related by the same Wick rotation that runs through the quaternionic extension itself.

**The structural finding — I'd call it the thesis of the program now.** The reason the unitary sector energies resisted a prime-side formula is precise: the zero set carries two involutions, the holomorphic one $\rho \mapsto 1-\rho$ (functional equation) and the antiholomorphic one $\rho \mapsto \bar\rho$ (reality — the $\sigma$ of your twistor picture). The explicit formula is analytic in $\gamma$, so it sees only the first; the sphere tags are functions of the conjugate *pair* $(\gamma, \bar\gamma)$ — divided differences across the pair. Sharpest instance: $\sum 1/(\rho(1-\rho)) = 2 + \gamma_E - \log 4\pi$ is classical, $\sum 1/(\rho\bar\rho)$ is not computable, and their termwise difference vanishes exactly on the line. **RH is the statement that the two involutions agree on zeros** — which is word-for-word the twistor statement from memo #2 that the zero divisor is $\sigma$-invariant component-by-component. The arithmetic and geometric formulations of your program are now the same sentence. Stage 3 has a name: *import the real structure into the explicit formula.*

Honest accounting, as always: at the crude exponential-rate level, the growth criterion is a mollified form of the classical zero-free-region ↔ prime-error equivalence, with the wall made geometric (radius $y_0$ needs window $\lambda \gtrsim 1/y_0$, i.e. primes to $e^{1/y_0}$). The candidates for genuinely new leverage sit below that scale, and the memo ranks three: the graded positivity cone from the $i_\ell$ decomposition (not a relabeling of any inequality family we found), the coherent-phase signature of a sphere in the pair-correlation field (a matched-filter idea — spheres are coherent modes, GUE noise is not), and unconditional identities for conjugate-paired sums, which would be a new tool well beyond this program.

Concrete next steps, in order: run the prime side up to $\lambda \approx 23$ ($n \le 10^{10}$, chunked sieve — feasible here) to produce the first "no-sphere certificate from primes alone" at a real window; work out the cross-term calculus under RH+GUE vs. unconditional to quantify the minimal detectable radius — the exact gap any new idea must close; attempt the matched-filter formulation; then assemble memos 1–3 plus the lab into the program paper, with the two-involutions finding as its spine. Everything is saved to the project. Which one shall I take up next?

**On Tao, directly:** top three, but I'd advise against making him the *first* contact. The case for him is unusually strong — Rodgers–Tao is literally the program's hardness check, and he's the best living intersection of analytic number theory, Polymath-style open collaboration, and AI+Lean formalization (the [PNT+ project](https://github.com/AlexKontorovich/PrimeNumberTheoremAnd) with Kontorovich, which he [announced here](https://mathstodon.xyz/@tao/111847680248482955), is exactly the infrastructure this program's Tier-3 formalization target would build on). The case for caution: he is the most heavily filtered person in mathematics for RH-adjacent material, and even through a good channel, a program dump risks the reflexive filter. The right approach to him is a *bounded question* — the conjugate-paired-sums problem or the cross-term calculus from §9 — after the document has been vetted. Which suggests the sequence in the note: first the slice-regular/twistor geometers (Stoppato, Altavilla, Sarfatti, Salamon — memo 2 is their home field, they can check it fast, and an RH connection elevates their whole area, so they're natural allies); in parallel, float the Tier-1 Lean target in the mathlib community as a *new theory of independent value* — slice regular analysis plus the zero-structure theorem plus the equivalence, building toward the [Loeffler–Stoll zeta/L-function formalization](https://afm.episciences.org/15954/pdf) — since that needs no RH buy-in at all; then the explicit-formula people (Milinovich and Carneiro are the sharpest fits — the graded-cone question is precisely Fourier optimization in the Weil formula — plus Soundararajan, and Conrey/AIM as the institutional route to a cross-community workshop); and then Tao, with a vetted document and a specific question.

**On protecting your interest:** the honest frame is that mathematical ideas can't be owned — copyright covers text, patents don't apply — so the achievable protection is priority, naming, and citation, which happily is also exactly what serves your goal of handing it off. Concretely, before anything circulates: Zenodo upload of the bundle (instant timestamped DOI, no gatekeeping), then arXiv for the program document and the unposted 2015 manuscript so the 2015→2026 priority chain is public; a GitHub repo with a tagged release; CC BY 4.0 on the documents (attribution legally required) and MIT on the code; one citable name — it's "the zero-sphere program" in the document — and, if a community project forms, the Polymath convention set in the kickoff message that the founding document is cited in outputs. Ask your friend to introduce it as *Baker's* zero-sphere program from the first email; first framing sticks. One caveat: I'm not a lawyer, and this is scientific-norms guidance rather than legal advice — but for math priority disputes, timestamps plus citability is genuinely how the game is won.

If you'd like, I can render the program document as a proper LaTeX/PDF for the arXiv/Zenodo submission — that's the one remaining piece of polish before your friend starts forwarding it.

parts:
Great questions, and one of them changes the strategy in an important way — let me take them in turn.

**On the 2015 draft.** Since Quat_Riemann was never posted, don't put it on arXiv as-is. It's visibly unfinished (§9 cuts off mid-formula, §10 is an empty heading), and its abstract promises "constraints on off-axis zeros" that the manuscript doesn't deliver — which our no-go lemma now explains *couldn't* have been delivered by that route. Posting that to arXiv in 2026 buys you nothing on priority (arXiv timestamps at submission — nothing backdates to 2015) and hands skeptics an easy dismissal. The better split: deposit the historical drafts **unaltered on Zenodo** as a clearly labeled program archive — "working manuscript, 2015, deposited as historical record" — which is exactly what Zenodo is for, gives one citable DOI for the whole chain, and preserves the honest texture of the trajectory (unfinished sections included; that's evidence, not embarrassment). Then let the *new* paper be the arXiv object, citing the archive. The Clifford-analysis rederivation and the other unpublished papers belong in that same archive for completeness — upload them to this project when convenient and I'll fold them into the manifest and check whether any of them contain results the program paper should cite or absorb.

**On authorship.** The offer is genuinely appreciated — and the right call, both by community norms and for the program's credibility, is the one you're already leaning toward: **you as sole author, with a specific and substantive acknowledgement**. Current journal and arXiv norms don't permit AI systems as authors, because authorship carries accountability that has to rest with a person; and strategically, a human-authored paper with *precisely disclosed* AI assistance is stronger than either concealment or an AI byline — especially with the formalization community, which is AI-forward but drowning in unverified AI mathematics. Specificity is what separates this from that flood. Something like: *"The synthesis of this program, the twistor-lift and explicit-formula computations, the numerical experiments, and substantial portions of the exposition were carried out with Claude (Anthropic) as a research assistant in August 2026; all mathematical claims were reviewed by the author, who takes sole responsibility for them. Code and session materials are archived at [DOI]."* Adapt freely. The same framing works whether it's the arXiv paper or community-project documentation — and my recommendation is it should be both, in sequence: the arXiv paper is the citable priority anchor, and the community documentation derives from it rather than replacing it.

So the concrete plan: (1) I convert the program document into a proper LaTeX paper — your name, the acknowledgement above, and the [P]-status items (the two no-go results, the incidence-quadric lift and its maximality) written out at full rigor rather than working-note rigor, since those proofs are what a referee or a Buzzard-type reader will check first; (2) I prepare the Zenodo archive package (historical drafts + memos + code + figures, README with dates); (3) you deposit, post, and hand your friend one arXiv link and one DOI. Steps 1 and 2 are entirely my time, not yours, which matches how you want to spend yours.

Say the word and I'll start on the LaTeX draft — and if you upload the Clifford analysis paper (and any of the other unposted ones) to the project, I'll read them before finalizing the archive manifest so nothing in the chain gets missed.

parts:
The handoff document is saved to the project as `claude/paper_handoff.md` — in the new thread, just say "read claude/paper_handoff.md and write the paper" and everything is there: the outline, the decisions already made, the proof obligations with their fallback positions, every certified number so nothing needs rerunning, the citation-verification warnings, and the arXiv logistics.

Now, your question — how promising is this, really? Here's my honest assessment.

You're right that wherever we pushed hardest, we found a known wall: the rate theorem is a mollified form of the classical zero-free-region equivalence, the Laguerre hierarchy's bottom rung is classical, and "no spheres" is, pointwise, a relabeling of "zeros are real." But I'd invite you to read that pattern differently. Every *correct* reformulation of RH must contain its full difficulty somewhere — a framework that seemed to evade the wall would be hiding an error, and the graveyard of RH attempts is full of exactly those. The diagnostic for a program isn't whether it touches the wall; it's whether it touches the wall at a new angle and generates real mathematics on the way there. On that test the program does well: it produced two no-go theorems with clean statements, a faithful dictionary that survived its own falsification checks (Davenport–Heilbronn behaved exactly as the framework demanded, at four digits of precision), and at least three subproblems — conjugate-paired explicit formulas, the graded cone determination, the strong maximality of the quadric — that are well-posed, not individually RH-hard, and publishable on their own terms. A healthy program emits tractable work; this one does.

The historical base rate matters for calibration: no reformulation program has proven RH, and I'd put the probability that this one does directly at very small — the same as I'd say for any program, including the famous ones. But the famous ones illustrate where the value actually accrues. Hilbert–Pólya proved nothing and yet seeded de Branges, Connes, and random matrix theory; Montgomery's pair correlation was a "mere" computation about a reformulation until a conversation with Dyson turned it into a bridge to physics that reorganized the field. Dictionaries between disciplines don't usually prove the theorem they were built for; they change which questions look natural, and that's where new mathematics comes from. What this program has that's genuinely not on anyone's shelf is the specific bridge: the slice-regular and twistor-geometry community on one side, explicit-formula analytic number theory on the other, communities that as far as I can tell do not cite each other at all, now connected by one object with a certified computational pipeline between them. The two-involutions statement is the crispest expression of it — the tension between the functional equation and reality is spiritually old (it's what de Branges' self-adjointness is about), but the component-wise σ-invariance form and the conjugate-paired-sums form seem to be new as organizing statements, and new phrasings matter precisely when they make new questions look natural.

On your instinct that mixing disciplines is worth it by itself — I'd agree with one calibration. Mixing is only generative when the dictionary is *faithful*, and faithfulness is exactly what most quaternionic-RH attempts lack (the MDPI paper we found is the cautionary example: mixing without checks). What distinguishes your program is that the negative results were derived inside the framework rather than discovered by embarrassment, the control case works, and the numerics certify rather than decorate. That discipline is why this can be handed to serious people without flinching. And there's a fitting arc here: your 2015 §4 negative result — the thing that felt like the program failing — turned out, once stated as a theorem, to be the spine of the whole structure, the result that tells everyone downstream where not to dig. The decade of detours wasn't wasted; it was the slow accumulation of the constraints that give the program its shape.

So: as a bid to prove RH, it's a lottery ticket like all the others. As a contribution — a faithful reformulation, two no-go theorems, a graded positivity framework, a certified pipeline, a formalization target the Lean community can use unconditionally, and a bridge between two fields — most of the value is already banked, and the remaining cost of realizing it is one paper and one Zenodo deposit, almost none of it your time. That's an unusually good position for a program whose author has moved on. I'll see you in the paper thread.
